text:
On the unseasonably warm midday of January 15, 1919, the North End of Boston was busy with ordinary life. Children were out of school for lunch, dockworkers were on their breaks, and horses and wagons crowded the streets near the harbor. Looming over the neighborhood, at 529 Commercial Street, stood a huge steel tank belonging to the Purity Distilling Company. It held more than two million gallons of molasses, a thick syrup that was shipped up from the Caribbean and used to make industrial alcohol and, in the case of rum, drink.

The tank had been built in 1915 by the United States Industrial Alcohol Company in a great hurry, to take advantage of wartime demand for the munitions that alcohol helped to produce. Its construction was careless. The steel was thinner than it should have been, no one properly tested it by filling it with water, and the company reportedly painted it brown so that the leaks would be harder to notice. Neighbors had long seen the tank groan and seep, and children sometimes collected the molasses that dribbled down its sides. Complaints went unanswered, and the company's response was largely cosmetic.

Just after 12:30 that afternoon, the tank gave way. Witnesses described a sound like a machine gun, which was the noise of rivets popping loose, followed by a low rumble as the steel burst apart. A wave of molasses perhaps fifteen feet high, by some accounts, rushed out at a speed estimated near thirty-five miles an hour. It tore buildings from their foundations, knocked a firehouse sideways, and buckled the girders of the elevated railway on Atlantic Avenue. Wagons, horses, and people were swept up in the flood, and many could not escape the sticky mass that swiftly thickened around them.

Twenty-one people died and about 150 were injured. Among the dead were children, city workers, and men who had been eating lunch near the firehouse. Rescuers waded into the syrup to reach survivors, and soldiers and sailors from nearby ships joined the effort. Police and Red Cross workers struggled for days to recover the victims, in some cases working through the molasses by hand. The cold winter air made the sticky mess harder to clear, and it clung to everything it touched. Cleanup crews spread sand and sawdust, and even used saltwater from fireboats to wash the streets. It was said that the harbor ran brown until summer, and that on hot days the neighborhood smelled sweet for decades.

The aftermath was as important as the disaster itself. The company at first blamed anarchists, suggesting that a bomb had destroyed the tank, a claim that fit the fears of the postwar era. But the families of the victims sued, and in one of the earliest major class-action suits in Massachusetts, an auditor spent years hearing testimony from hundreds of witnesses. Engineers showed that the tank had been poorly designed and that its safety margins were far too thin. In 1925 the court found the company responsible, and it paid roughly six hundred thousand dollars in settlements.

The flood changed American law and engineering. It pushed Massachusetts to require licensed professionals to sign off on building plans, and it helped establish the idea that companies could not shrug off responsibility for dangerous structures. Today, only a small plaque near the site recalls what happened, but the Great Molasses Flood remains a striking reminder of how ordinary materials, handled carelessly, can become deadly.
